text: The real remedy is to store not the dense $A_n$ but only the "standard" monomials. With an ordering compatible with multiplication (deg-lex), a monomial that leads a row of $J$ with an invertible coefficient stays leading with an invertible coefficient in all multiples $u\,w\,v$ as well, so it is eliminated together with them. What remains is an order ideal of monomials, of size at least $\dim_{\mathbb F_p}\Delta_{\mathbb F_p}/\Delta_{\mathbb F_p}^n$ (§6.4). This is the nilpotent quotient algorithm for an associative algebra, but over the ring $\mathbb Z/p^E$ rather than over a field as in ModIsom. It is not part of the prototype (§6).

At small orders (256, 512) A in C is faster than the Python variant B: there $M$ is comparable to $|G|$ (for groups of order 256 with $d=6$ at $n=5$ $M=1554>255$), and Python has a fixed overhead per group. At order 2187 B is 30 times faster than A in C, and hundreds of times faster than numpy.

For the group of order $3^{494}$ the indices $\log_3|\Delta/\Delta^n|=59, 321, 1430$ ($n=2,3,4$) agreed modulo $3^{19}$ and over $\mathbb Z$. On the 394 tested elements (pcgs of layers 2–4) $D_n=\gamma_n$ for $n\le4$, consistent with Passi's theorem ($D_4=\gamma_4$ for odd $p$).
